summary: Describes the Direct Data Placement protocol, which carries information that allows incoming data to be placed directly in an upper layer's receive buffer. It reduces CPU and memory use. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Instead of leaving packages in a hallway first, deliver them right to the room where they belong.

questions: what is an stag in ddp
what is the difference between tagged and untagged buffers
how does ddp avoid copying data
subtitle: A header format that lets a network card write incoming data straight into the application's own buffer, without an extra copy.

tldr.problem: When incoming data lands in an intermediate buffer and then has to be copied to its final place, the copy costs CPU cycles and memory bandwidth and caps throughput at the speed the CPU can copy.
tldr.mechanism: Each DDP segment carries a small header saying exactly where its payload belongs, either in a named Tagged Buffer (STag plus offset) or in the next queued Untagged Buffer (queue number, message sequence number, offset). The receiver can place data even if segments arrive out of order.
tldr.outcome: Data is placed once, in its final destination, while delivery to the upper layer stays in order. DDP is part of the iWARP suite, and the RFC has since been updated by RFC 7146.

today: RFC 5041 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7146. The unit metadata does not list it as obsoleted.

sections.title: What Direct Data Placement Does
sections.content:
The Direct Data Placement protocol (DDP) lets an Upper Layer Protocol (ULP) send data to a Data Sink without the Data Sink first placing it in an intermediate buffer. When the data arrives, the network interface can place it directly in the ULP's buffer. The RFC says this uses substantially less memory bandwidth and substantially fewer CPU cycles, and removes the limit of moving data only as fast as the CPU can copy it.

DDP preserves ULP message boundaries. It has two buffer models, the Tagged and the Untagged Buffer Model, provides reliable in-order delivery semantics for both, and segments and reassembles messages. A ULP message may contain up to 2^32 - 1 octets of payload.

The RFC separates Placement (writing payload into a buffer, which can happen in any order) from Delivery (telling the ULP a message is complete, which is strictly ordered). That split lets the ULP buffer double as the reassembly buffer, even when segments arrive out of order.
sections.eli5: DDP puts each piece of a delivery straight into the right spot instead of piling it in a hallway first. Only when the whole delivery is done and the earlier ones are done does it ring the bell.

sections.title: Where DDP Sits in the Stack
sections.content:
DDP is meant to be independent of the Lower Layer Protocol (LLP), subject to the requirements in the RFC. It is specified as part of a family designed to work together. Over TCP, DDP uses Marker PDU Aligned Framing (MPA, RFC 5044). Over SCTP it uses the SCTP DDP adaptation (RFC 5043). Above DDP sits the Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol (RDMAP, RFC 5040), and the suite of RDMAP, DDP and MPA is called iWARP.

A DDP Stream maps to one LLP Stream. For SCTP, a DDP Stream maps directly to an SCTP stream. For MPA, it maps to a TCP connection and a single DDP Stream is supported. DDP gives no ordering guarantees between DDP Streams. The specification requires a reliable, in-order LLP.
sections.eli5: DDP is a middle layer in a sandwich. The bread below carries the packages reliably, and the filling above decides what the packages are for.

sections.title: What DDP Needs from the Layer Below
sections.content:
Any protocol serving as an LLP MUST meet a list of requirements. The main ones:

  • It MUST expose the MULPDU, the current maximum record size, and its changes, and MUST NOT force DDP to re-segment segments already posted.
  • If it accepts a DDP Segment it MUST deliver it reliably or report an error, and MUST preserve segment and message boundaries.
  • It MAY hand up segments out of order for Placement, but then MUST also give the sender-specified order.
  • It MUST provide a strong digest, at least equivalent to CRC32-C, covering at least the DDP Segment, because direct memory writes need a stronger check than a simple checksum.
  • It MUST provide the length of each received segment, so DDP needs no length field in its header.
  • It MUST NOT pass a duplicate segment up after the earlier ones were passed.

It must also signal graceful teardown of streams and connections, and label a stream erroneous after a DDP error if streams cannot be torn down independently.
sections.eli5: DDP trusts the delivery service below it to bring every package intact, tell it how big each one is and keep the boxes from being split or repeated. Without that, DDP cannot do its job.

sections.title: The DDP Headers
sections.content:
Every DDP Segment MUST have a DDP Header, and may carry ULP payload. The first 8 bits are a common Control Field: T (1 bit, Tagged), L (1 bit, Last), Rsvd (4 bits, zero on transmit) and DV (2 bits, version, which MUST be 1). L MUST be set on the last segment of every message and on no other.

The Tagged header adds an 8-bit RsvdULP, a 32-bit STag (Steering Tag) naming the receiver's buffer, and a 64-bit TO (Tagged Offset) giving where in that buffer placement starts. A message MAY start at an arbitrary TO.

The Untagged header adds a 40-bit RsvdULP, a 32-bit QN (Queue Number) choosing a receive queue, a 32-bit MSN (Message Sequence Number) and a 32-bit MO (Message Offset). MSN starts at one, increases by one for each message on the queue, and wraps to 0 after 0xFFFFFFFF. Every segment in a message MUST carry the same STag, QN or MSN values.
sections.eli5: Each piece carries a label. A tagged label says which box and where inside it. An untagged label says which line, which number in the line, and how far into the message this piece is.

sections.title: Moving, Splitting and Delivering Data
sections.content:
In the Tagged Buffer Model, the Data Sink advertises a buffer (its STag, address and length) using a ULP-specific method, and the Data Source then writes into it at offsets it chooses. One advertisement can serve several messages. In the Untagged Buffer Model, the Data Sink queues receive buffers and each arriving message consumes the next one; a message can only start at offset 0, and one too large for the buffer is an error.

DDP MUST segment each message so every segment fits within the MULPDU advertised by the LLP. For untagged messages, the first-segment example in the RFC is 2048 octets with a MULPDU of 1500: one segment at MO 0 with 1482 octets and a second at MO 1482 with 566 octets. A zero-length message is allowed and uses exactly one segment.

At the Data Source, messages MUST be sent in submission order. At the Data Sink, DDP MAY place segments out of order or more than once, MUST deliver a message at most once and MUST deliver messages in the order sent. It delivers a message only when its last segment arrived, all its segments are placed, and all earlier messages are placed and delivered.
sections.eli5: Big deliveries are cut into pieces that fit in the truck. Each piece says where it goes, so the pieces can be unloaded in any order, but the customer is only told once everything for that order has arrived.

sections.title: Teardown and Error Handling
sections.content:
DDP MUST NOT start closing a stream on its own; it follows the LLP or the ULP. Both endpoints must enable and tear down DDP at the same time so that the Data Sink does not misread segments. After a graceful close request from the LLP, any further received data is an error and MUST cause an abortive teardown.

Before placing a segment, the Data Sink MUST validate it. For untagged segments it checks the QN, that a buffer is associated with the QN and MSN, that the MO and the payload length plus MO fall in the legal range, and that the MSN is in the legal range. For tagged segments it checks the STag, its associated buffer, that the TO and the length plus TO are in the registered range, and that the 64-bit sum does not wrap.

On any such error DDP MUST stop placing the segment, report it to the ULP and silently drop later segments. It SHOULD let the ULP send one more message before the stream ends.
sections.eli5: Before putting a package in a room, the receiver checks that the room exists, the label makes sense and the package fits. If something is wrong, it stops, tells the boss and ignores more packages from that line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because DDP exposes memory addresses on the wire, a third party injecting spoofed packets could try to corrupt memory at a Data Sink. The placement information in each segment must therefore be validated, including the STag and an octet-level base and bounds check, before any data is placed.

The RFC requires two ways to associate an STag with a DDP Stream: a Protection Domain association and a DDP Stream association. If an incoming tagged segment's stream does not match the STag, it is not placed and DDP MUST report a local error. STags are valid only for the exact byte range and the duration set by the ULP, and the ULP can revoke them. The RFC also sets requirements for the RDMA-enabled NIC (RNIC) and a Privileged Resource Manager.

DDP does not itself authenticate the LLP stream, so the ULP is responsible for that. If impersonation or hijacking is possible, authentication, integrity and replay protection are highly RECOMMENDED. IPsec can be used with ESP, and the RFC follows the IPsec profile of RFC 3723. A longer analysis is in RFC 5042.
sections.eli5: Since the labels say exactly where to put things in memory, a prankster could send fake labels. So the receiver checks every label, only opens the rooms it was told to open, and can lock a room again at any time.
